extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduates/graduate students and general readers of physics and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of kinematics: definitions and fundamental propositions connecting curvature, velocity, and acceleration, plus philosophical remarks about the conceptual status of motion and matter. Intended as a textbook-style treatment of point-motion and methods for constructing motion from simpler components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular measure and radian
rubrics_metrics.description: The circular measure c of any angle is the ratio of the arc a subtended by this angle at the centre of any circle to the radius r of this circle; the unit for which a equals r is the radian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines angle measure in radians (c = a/r). Use radians in theoretical investigations; the radian is the natural unit because it relates arc length directly to radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean curvature of an arc
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean curvature over any arc ab of a circle centre O is the ratio of the angle between the tangents at its extremities (equivalently the central angle) to the length of the arc ab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a circle this mean curvature equals the inverse of the radius and is independent of the arc length. This motivates the radius of curvature concept: at any point of a curve a circle of appropriate radius fits most closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual curvature as measurable slope on curvature-chart
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual curvature at a point is the limit of the mean curvature over vanishingly small arcs and is measurable as the slope (to the vertical) of the tangent to the corresponding point on the curvature-chart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat curvature as a local, measurable quantity obtained as a limit of mean curvatures; use curvature-charts (graphical representations) to visualize and measure local curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature equals spin of tangent divided by speed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point moves along a curve the ratio of the spin of the tangent to the speed of the point is the actual curvature at each situation of the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed symbolically as curvature = S / U where S is instantaneous spin (rate of turning of tangent) and U is speed. This connects purely geometric notion (curvature) with kinematic rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal (shunt) acceleration relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The shunt (normal) acceleration in the case considered is properly measured by the product of curvature and the square of the speed; equivalently normal acceleration = U^2 / r = S × U = U • S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides three equivalent expressions: v^2/r, curvature×v^2, and spin×speed. Direction: perpendicular to the direction of motion. Use to compute centripetal/normal acceleration from path geometry and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition of acceleration into spurt and shunt
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceleration has spurt (tangential) and shunt (normal) components: the spurt takes place in the direction of motion and is measured by the rate of change of speed; the shunt takes place perpendicular to motion and is measured by curvature × speed^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing motion, separate tangential (affecting speed) and normal (affecting direction) components. In limiting construction, rotations of velocity vectors correspond to shunt, stretches to spurt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero acceleration implies straight-line uniform motion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point be not accelerated it will describe a straight line with uniform speed; there will be no spurt (so speed uniform) and no shunt (so curvature zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither uniform speed alone nor zero curvature alone implies absence of acceleration; both components must vanish for zero acceleration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal acceleration for constrained motion
rubrics_metrics.description: When a point is constrained to move in a given path the normal acceleration may be determined in each position from the speed and the form of the path (its curvature). The problem then is to find the speed from the speed-acceleration (tangential) information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For constrained motion (given path), geometry provides normal acceleration; dynamic problem reduces to integrating tangential acceleration to obtain speed along the known path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of motion from initial velocity and acceleration field
rubrics_metrics.description: When a point is free to move in a given plane, its motion can be theoretically determined if we know its velocity in any one position and its acceleration for all positions; from these one can construct the path and time-chart to any desired accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the foundational Cauchy-type statement for kinematics: initial state + acceleration field determines motion. Practically, construction requires mathematical analysis (integrating acceleration) and can be approximated by successive small elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of time-chart by successive elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing the path and the speed at each point, one can construct a time-chart by drawing successive little elements whose slopes are given by local speeds; by taking sufficiently small elements the polygonal approximation approaches the true curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes a practical geometric method of stepwise construction: use local slope from speed to draw element, project horizontally to get next position and speed, iterate to build time-chart. Emphasizes limiting process for accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram law for combining displacements, velocities, accelerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The displacement (and in the limit velocity) of P relative to O' equals the geometric (parallelogram) sum of the displacement/velocity of P relative to O and of O relative to O'; the same holds for accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret mean quantities as sides of a triangle; in the limit obtain vector addition of velocities and accelerations. Use parallelogram (vector) addition to change reference frames and synthesize independent motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis of complex motions from simple components
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the parallelogram rule lies in building up complex cases of motion from simple ones; if perceptual antecedents of different accelerations superpose without altering values, their accelerations add geometrically (superposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply superposition (vector addition) when independent causes/accelerations can be superposed. Example: application of law of gravitation to planetary theory as synthesis of elemental accelerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of motion and frame dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: All motion is relative: absolute velocity and absolute acceleration are meaningless; velocities and accelerations are described relative to a chosen pole (origin), and transformations between poles follow the parallelogram law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing reference frame, add relative-frame velocity/acceleration vectors geometrically. Mean/actual velocities form corresponding triangles whose sides are proportional to displacements; frame-choice is arbitrary but transforms predictably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual status of motion and geometrical ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion (and the geometrical forms used to describe it) is essentially a conceptual construct, not itself a direct perceptual datum; space and time are modes under which we perceive, and motion is a mode of perception rather than a perceptual object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat motion as a symbolic, ideal representation used to describe changes in sense-impressions. Beware of conflating conceptual models (points, rigid bodies, etc.) with perceptual reality; this has methodological consequences for interpreting laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframing the three problems about motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The three natural questions — What moves? Why does it move? How does it move? — must be distinguished between conceptual and perceptual spheres; in the conceptual sphere they have clear answers (points, rigid bodies, strainable media move; modes of motion describe how), while asked of perception they are unanswerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When posing foundational questions, clarify whether they are about conceptual representation (answerable within theory) or about perceptual reality (where such questions may be ill-posed). This reframing avoids metaphysical confusions (e.g., about 'force' as metaphysical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of naive definitions of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook-style assertions such as 'Matter is a primary conception of the human mind' are obscure and paralogistic; one must avoid circular definitions (e.g., matter is that which moves) and seek clearer, non-question-begging characterizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages critical scrutiny of definitions in physics: do not accept circular or metaphysical definitions; demand operational/conceptual clarity about what is being posited (matter as conceptual construct vs perceptual datum).
